claim: C. elegans alternate between roaming states, characterized by high-speed forward movement and occasional reorientations, and dwelling states, marked by slow forward and backward movements while foraging on bacterial food.
source: While foraging on bacterial food, C. elegans alternate between roaming states, characterized by high-speed forward movement and occasional reorientations, and dwelling states, marked by slow forward and backward movements (Ben Arous et al., 2009; Fujiwara et al., 2002; Flavell et al., 2020; Kim and Flavell, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Ben Arous et al., 2009; Fujiwara et al., 2002; Flavell et al., 2020; Kim and Flavell, 2020) that have characterized these behavioral states.

claim: Each roaming or dwelling state can last up to tens of minutes.
source: Each state can last up to tens of minutes and the transitions between states are abrupt.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations in the surrounding context and is consistent with the data shown in the manuscript.

claim: The transitions between roaming and dwelling states are abrupt.
source: Each state can last up to tens of minutes and the transitions between states are abrupt.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations in the surrounding context and is consistent with the data shown in the manuscript.

claim: The fraction of time an animal spends in roaming versus dwelling is influenced by its satiety, ingestion of bacterial food, and sensory cues such as odors.
source: The fraction of time an animal spends in each state is influenced by its satiety, ingestion of bacterial food, and sensory cues such as odors (Ben Arous et al., 2009; Fujiwara et al., 2002; Chew et al., 2018; Shtonda and Avery, 2006; Rhoades et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Ben Arous et al., 2009; Fujiwara et al., 2002; Chew et al., 2018; Shtonda and Avery, 2006; Rhoades et al., 2019).

claim: Animals favor dwelling in food-rich environments and after starvation.
source: Consistent with the notion that these states reflect an exploration-exploitation tradeoff, animals favor dwelling in food-rich environments and after starvation, but favor roaming in poor-quality food environments and after aversive stimulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by the context of previous studies and is consistent with the exploration-exploitation framework.

claim: Animals favor roaming in poor-quality food environments and after aversive stimulation.
source: Consistent with the notion that these states reflect an exploration-exploitation tradeoff, animals favor dwelling in food-rich environments and after starvation, but favor roaming in poor-quality food environments and after aversive stimulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by the context of previous studies and is consistent with the exploration-exploitation framework.

claim: Serotonin (5-HT) and the neuropeptide pigment-dispersing factor (PDF) act as opposing neuromodulators that stabilize dwelling and roaming states, respectively.
source: We and others previously found that serotonin (5-HT) and the neuropeptide pigment-dispersing factor (PDF) act as opposing neuromodulators that stabilize dwelling and roaming states, respectively (Rhoades et al., 2019; Choi et al., 2013; Flavell et al., 2013; Sawin et al., 2000; Iwanir et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Rhoades et al., 2019; Choi et al., 2013; Flavell et al., 2013; Sawin et al., 2000; Iwanir et al., 2016).

claim: Serotonin acts through the serotonin-gated chloride channel MOD-1 to promote dwelling, with a smaller contribution from other serotonin receptors.
source: Serotonin acts through the serotonin-gated chloride channel MOD-1 to promote dwelling, with a smaller contribution from the other serotonin receptors (Flavell et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Flavell et al., 2013).

claim: PDF-1 and PDF-2 neuropeptides act through a single PDF receptor, PDFR-1, to drive roaming.
source: PDF-1 and –2 neuropeptides act through a single PDF receptor, PDFR-1, to drive roaming (Flavell et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Flavell et al., 2013).

claim: Six of the 10 recorded neurons displayed calcium levels that correlated with axial velocity and movement direction.
source: Six of the 10 recorded neurons displayed calcium levels that correlated with axial velocity and movement direction (Figure 1D–E; Figure 1—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D-E and Figure 1—figure supplement 5A.

claim: The PDF-1-expressing neuron AVB and PDFR-1-expressing neurons AIY and RIB exhibited increased activity during forward runs.
source: Consistent with previous reports, we observed that the PDF-1-expressing neuron AVB and PDFR-1-expressing neurons AIY and RIB, known to promote forward runs (Kato et al., 2015; Roberts et al., 2016; Li et al., 2014; Tsalik and Hobert, 2003; Gray et al., 2005; Luo et al., 2014), exhibited increased activity during forward runs, while the premotor neuron AVA, known to promote reversals (Kato et al., 2015; Roberts et al., 2016; Luo et al., 2014; Chalfie et al., 1985), exhibited heightened activity during reversals.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Kato et al., 2015; Roberts et al., 2016; Li et al., 2014; Tsalik and Hobert, 2003; Gray et al., 2005; Luo et al., 2014) and is consistent with the data presented.

claim: The premotor neuron AVA exhibited heightened activity during reversals.
source: Consistent with previous reports, we observed that the PDF-1-expressing neuron AVB and PDFR-1-expressing neurons AIY and RIB, known to promote forward runs (Kato et al., 2015; Roberts et al., 2016; Li et al., 2014; Tsalik and Hobert, 2003; Gray et al., 2005; Luo et al., 2014), exhibited increased activity during forward runs, while the premotor neuron AVA, known to promote reversals (Kato et al., 2015; Roberts et al., 2016; Luo et al., 2014; Chalfie et al., 1985), exhibited heightened activity during reversals.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Kato et al., 2015; Roberts et al., 2016; Luo et al., 2014; Chalfie et al., 1985) and is consistent with the data presented.

claim: Nine of the ten recorded neurons exhibited changes in activity as animals transitioned between roaming and dwelling states.
source: Moreover, we found that nine of the ten recorded neurons exhibited changes in activity as animals transitioned between roaming and dwelling states (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: Almost all neurons whose activity correlated with axial velocity and/or movement direction, in particular AVB, AIY, RIB, and AVA, exhibited reduced activity during dwelling, compared to roaming.
source: Interestingly, almost all neurons whose activity correlated with axial velocity and/or movement direction, in particular AVB, AIY, RIB, and AVA, exhibited reduced activity during dwelling, compared to roaming (overall and/or surrounding moments of state transitions; Figure 1D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: The serotonergic neuron NSM was more active during dwelling.
source: In contrast, the serotonergic neuron NSM was more active during dwelling.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D-E and other figures in the manuscript.

claim: The top two principal components (PC1 and PC2) explained 44% of the total variance in neural activity.
source: Indeed, the top two principal components (PC1 and PC2), which together explained 44% of the total variance, exhibited clear behavioral correlates (Figure 1F–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by the PCA analysis described in the text and shown in Figure 1F-G.

claim: Neural activity along PC1 was coupled to the animal's forward and reverse locomotion.
source: Neural activity along PC1 was coupled to the animal's forward and reverse locomotion (Figure 1F), while activity along PC2 was coupled to the animal's axial speed and foraging state (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Activity along PC2 was coupled to the animal's axial speed and foraging state.
source: Neural activity along PC1 was coupled to the animal's forward and reverse locomotion (Figure 1F), while activity along PC2 was coupled to the animal's axial speed and foraging state (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: PC1 consisted of positive contributions from forward-run-active neurons (e.g. AVB, AIY, RIB, and RME), a negative contribution from the reversal-active neuron AVA, and almost no contribution from the serotonergic neuron NSM.
source: PC1 consisted of positive contributions from forward-run-active neurons (e.g. AVB, AIY, RIB, and RME), a negative contribution from the reversal-active neuron AVA, and almost no contribution from the serotonergic neuron NSM (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7.

claim: PC2 consisted of a strong positive contribution from NSM and negative contributions from both forward-run- and reversal-active neurons.
source: In contrast, PC2 consisted of a strong positive contribution from NSM, which is active at low speeds, and negative contributions from both forward-run- and reversal-active neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7.

claim: A nonlinear regression model was able to predict animal velocity from concurrent neural activity data with a high degree of accuracy.
source: A nonlinear regression model was able to predict animal velocity from concurrent neural activity data with a high degree of accuracy (Figure 1H).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: A logistic regression model trained to predict the roaming and dwelling state achieved over 95% accuracy when using activity from all 10 neurons.
source: In addition, a logistic regression model trained to predict the roaming and dwelling state achieved over 95 % accuracy when using activity from all 10 neurons, and exhibited classification accuracy significantly above baseline when using data from only NSM or the roaming-active neurons AIY, RIB, and AVB (Figure 1I).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: A logistic regression model exhibited classification accuracy significantly above baseline when using data from only NSM or the roaming-active neurons AIY, RIB, and AVB.
source: In addition, a logistic regression model trained to predict the roaming and dwelling state achieved over 95 % accuracy when using activity from all 10 neurons, and exhibited classification accuracy significantly above baseline when using data from only NSM or the roaming-active neurons AIY, RIB, and AVB (Figure 1I).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: NSM activity was increased during dwelling as compared to roaming.
source: NSM activity was increased during dwelling as compared to roaming, resulting in a negative correlation with animal speed, which differs across the two states (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: NSM activity was not correlated with speed within the roaming state.
source: However, NSM activity was not correlated with speed within the roaming state and it was not associated with movement direction during any state (Figures 2A and 1D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 2A and 1D-E.

claim: NSM activity was not associated with movement direction during any state.
source: However, NSM activity was not correlated with speed within the roaming state and it was not associated with movement direction during any state (Figures 2A and 1D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 2A and 1D-E.

claim: An increase in NSM activity consistently preceded dwelling, with an average latency of 23 s.
source: An increase in NSM activity consistently preceded dwelling, with an average latency of 23 s (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B-C.

claim: Dwelling states frequently ended with a decrease in NSM activity, though with a more variable latency.
source: Dwelling states frequently ended with a decrease in NSM activity, though with a more variable latency (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Across wild-type animals, the durations of individual dwelling states were positively correlated with the durations of co-occurring bouts of NSM activity.
source: Across wild-type animals, the durations of individual dwelling states were positively correlated with the durations of co-occurring bouts of NSM activity, which both typically lasted many minutes (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of NSM inhibited the activity of the roaming-active neurons AVB, AIY, and RIB and led to a decrease in animal speed.
source: Indeed, optogenetic stimulation of NSM (performed at a low all-trans-retinal (ATR) concentration to avoid background activation; see Materials and methods) inhibited the activity of the roaming-active neurons AVB, AIY, and RIB and led to a decrease in animal speed (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The effects of optogenetic NSM stimulation on roaming-active neurons and animal speed were largely abolished in mutants lacking the 5-HT-gated chloride channel mod-1.
source: These effects were largely abolished in mutants lacking the 5-HT-gated chloride channel mod-1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), consistent with previous reports that the mod-1 receptor is critical for 5-HT-induced locomotion changes (Flavell et al., 2013; Sawin et al., 2000; Iwanir et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and citations to previous studies (Flavell et al., 2013; Sawin et al., 2000; Iwanir et al., 2016).

claim: Mutants that disrupt 5-HT signaling, such as those lacking a key enzyme for serotonin biosynthesis (tph-1) or a 5-HT-gated chloride channel (mod-1), exhibited a decrease in time spent in the dwelling state.
source: Mutants that disrupt 5-HT signaling, such as those lacking a key enzyme for serotonin biosynthesis (tph-1) or a 5-HT-gated chloride channel (mod-1), exhibited a decrease in time spent in the dwelling state (Figure 3A–B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 2), consistent with previous results (Flavell et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A-B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, and a citation to a previous study (Flavell et al., 2013).

claim: In wild-type animals, NSM activity was strongly associated with reduced speed, but this relationship was attenuated in tph-1 and mod-1 mutants.
source: In wild-type animals, NSM activity was strongly associated with reduced speed, but this relationship was attenuated in tph-1 and mod-1 mutants (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The durations of the NSM activity bouts were dramatically shortened in tph-1 and mod-1 mutants.
source: Surprisingly, we also found that the durations of the NSM activity bouts, which were minutes-long in wild-type animals, were dramatically shortened in these mutants (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: There was a significant decrease in the fraction of time that NSM is active in tph-1 and mod-1 mutants.
source: This resulted in a significant decrease in the fraction of time that NSM is active in the mutants (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: 5-HT signaling is required to sustain the activity of the serotonergic neuron NSM.
source: These results indicate that 5-HT signaling is required to sustain the activity of the serotonergic neuron NSM.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing that NSM activity bouts are shortened in tph-1 and mod-1 mutants.

claim: Activation of mod-1-expressing neurons inhibits NSM activity.
source: To directly test whether activation of these neurons inhibits NSM, we activated the mod-1-expressing neurons with Chrimson while recording NSM activity. We delivered the optogenetic stimuli specifically when NSM activity was high and observed a sustained inhibition of NSM activity throughout the stimulation (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The serotonergic NSM neuron promotes its own activity via mutual inhibition with neurons expressing the inhibitory 5-HT receptor MOD-1.
source: Together, these results indicate that the serotonergic NSM neuron promotes its own activity via mutual inhibition with neurons expressing the inhibitory 5-HT receptor MOD-1 (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing that NSM activity is reduced in mod-1 mutants and that optogenetic activation of mod-1-expressing neurons inhibits NSM.

claim: In wild-type animals, the serotonergic neuron NSM and the PDF-1-producing neuron AVB exhibited a mutually exclusive activity pattern.
source: In wild-type animals, the serotonergic neuron NSM and the PDF-1-producing neuron AVB exhibited a mutually exclusive activity pattern, wherein NSM activity was high and AVB activity was low during dwelling, while NSM activity was low and AVB was dynamically active during roaming (Figure 4C; here we define 'mutual exclusivity' to be a lack of concurrent high activity in NSM and AVB; see Materials and methods and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A for thresholding approach to segment low versus high activity).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The mutual exclusivity between NSM and AVB activity was strongly disrupted in pdfr-1 mutants.
source: This mutual exclusivity was strongly disrupted in pdfr-1 mutants (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: In pdfr-1 mutants, NSM and AVB were frequently co-active, giving rise to a positive correlation between the activities of the two neurons.
source: In these mutant animals, the two neurons were frequently co-active, giving rise to a positive correlation between the activities of the two neurons (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: pdfr-1 animals frequently moved at speeds mid-way between those typically seen for roaming and dwelling states in wild-type animals.
source: We observed that pdfr-1 animals frequently moved at speeds mid-way between those typically seen for roaming and dwelling states in wild-type animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 5A-B; this observation prompted us to not perform roaming-dwelling state calls on the pdfr-1 mutant).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5A-B.

claim: PDF signaling is required for the neural circuit to maintain mutual exclusivity between NSM and the locomotion-controlling neurons that are active during roaming.
source: These findings indicate that PDF signaling is required for the neural circuit to maintain mutual exclusivity between NSM and the locomotion-controlling neurons that are active during roaming.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing that mutual exclusivity is disrupted in pdfr-1 mutants.

claim: NSM activity bouts in pdfr-1 mutants were more persistent than they were in wild-type animals.
source: In contrast to the tph-1 animals, NSM activity bouts in pdfr-1 mutants were more persistent than they were in wild-type animals (Figure 4E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E-F.

claim: PDF signaling plays an important role in suppressing NSM activity.
source: This result suggests that PDF signaling plays an important role in suppressing NSM activity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing that NSM activity bouts are more persistent in pdfr-1 mutants.

claim: Constitutive activation of PDFR-1 signaling, via expression of the hyperactive PDFR-1 effector ACY-1(P260S) in the pdfr-1-expressing neurons, strongly inhibited NSM activity.
source: Consistent with this interpretation, constitutive activation of PDFR-1 signaling, via expression of the hyperactive PDFR-1 effector ACY-1(P260S) in the pdfr-1-expressing neurons, strongly inhibited NSM activity (Figure 4B; Figure 4E–F; Figure 4—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4B, Figure 4E-F, and Figure 4—figure supplement 4B.

claim: Optogenetic activation of the pdf-1-expressing neurons led to an acute and robust inhibition of NSM.
source: In addition, optogenetic activation of the pdf-1-expressing neurons led to an acute and robust inhibition of NSM (Figure 4G; Figure 4—figure supplement 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 5C.

claim: PDF signaling is necessary and sufficient to keep NSM inactive during roaming.
source: Together, these findings indicate that PDF signaling is necessary and sufficient to keep NSM inactive during roaming, a key requirement for generating the opposing roaming and dwelling states.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing that NSM activity is increased in pdfr-1 mutants and that optogenetic activation of pdf-1-expressing neurons inhibits NSM.

claim: tph-1;pdfr-1 double mutants exhibited prolonged bouts of NSM activation, an increased probability of NSM being active, and a near two-fold increase in the probability of co-activation between NSM and AVB.
source: Similar to the pdfr-1 single mutants, these animals exhibited prolonged bouts of NSM activation, an increased probability of NSM being active, and a near two-fold increase in the probability of co-activation between NSM and AVB (Figure 4C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C-F.

claim: tph-1;pdfr-1 animals spent over a third of their time moving at intermediate speeds, similar to the pdfr-1 animals.
source: At the behavioral level, tph-1;pdfr-1 animals spent over a third of their time moving at intermediate speeds, similar to the pdfr-1 animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 5A-B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5A-B.

claim: pdfr-1 functions downstream of tph-1 to control NSM activity and locomotion.
source: Together, these results suggest that pdfr-1 functions downstream of tph-1 to control NSM activity and locomotion.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the epistasis analysis showing that tph-1;pdfr-1 double mutants resemble pdfr-1 single mutants.

claim: Optogenetic activation of the mod-1-expressing neurons, which triggered high-speed locomotion in wild-type animals, failed to do so in pdfr-1 mutants.
source: We found that optogenetic activation of the mod-1-expressing neurons, which triggered high-speed locomotion in wild-type animals, failed to do so in pdfr-1 mutants (Figure 4H).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The pdfr-1-expressing neurons act downstream of the mod-1-expressing neurons to promote roaming.
source: These results indicate that the pdfr-1-expressing neurons act downstream of the mod-1-expressing neurons to promote roaming (Figure 4I), consistent with the epistasis analysis described above.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing that optogenetic activation of mod-1-expressing neurons fails to induce high-speed locomotion in pdfr-1 mutants.

claim: The mutually inhibitory interaction between NSM and the neurons that express the MOD-1 and PDFR-1 receptors is necessary to stabilize the opposing neural activity and behavioral patterns underlying roaming and dwelling.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that the mutually inhibitory interaction between NSM and the neurons that express the MOD-1 and PDFR-1 receptors is necessary to stabilize the opposing neural activity and behavioral patterns underlying roaming and dwelling.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing that disrupting 5-HT or PDF signaling alters the persistence and mutual exclusivity of NSM and roaming-active neuron activity.

claim: Successfully trained CNN networks achieved over 70% test accuracy in predicting NSM activation.
source: Successfully trained networks achieved over 70 % test accuracy, equaling or exceeding other supervised learning methods (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Stereotyped circuit activity patterns frequently precede NSM activation.
source: This result indicates that stereotyped circuit activity patterns frequently precede NSM activation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the high test accuracy of the CNN classifier.

claim: Successfully trained CNNs consistently employed a convolutional filter where the largest positive weights were associated with the sensory processing neuron AIA and the largest negative weights were linked to RIB and AVA.
source: Successfully trained networks consistently employed a convolutional filter where the largest positive weights were associated with the sensory processing neuron AIA and the largest negative weights were linked to RIB and AVA, which promote forward and reverse movement, respectively (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: NSM activation is most likely to occur following increased activity in AIA and decreased activity in RIB and AVA.
source: These weights suggest that NSM activation is most likely to occur following increased activity in AIA and decreased activity in RIB and AVA.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the convolutional filter weights identified by the CNN.

claim: Withholding AIA, RIB, and AVA from the training data abolished the predictive power of the trained network.
source: Withholding AIA, RIB, and AVA from the training data abolished the predictive power of the trained network, while withholding AIA activity alone also led to a significant reduction in test accuracy (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Networks trained on the activities of only AIA, RIB, and AVA performed nearly as well as those trained on all the neurons.
source: Moreover, networks trained on the activities of only AIA, RIB, and AVA performed nearly as well as those trained on all the neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The combined activities of AIA, RIB, and AVA can frequently predict the onset of NSM activity, which is strongly associated with roaming-to-dwelling state transitions.
source: These observations suggest that the combined activities of AIA, RIB, and AVA can frequently predict the onset of NSM activity, which is strongly associated with roaming-to-dwelling state transitions.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the CNN analysis showing that AIA, RIB, and AVA activities are sufficient to predict NSM activation.

claim: During roaming, AIA activity was positively correlated with that of forward run-promoting neurons, such as RIB, and negatively correlated with the reversal-promoting neuron AVA.
source: During roaming, AIA activity was positively correlated with that of forward run-promoting neurons, such as RIB, and negatively correlated with the reversal-promoting neuron AVA.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C-G.

claim: Within 30 s of NSM activation, AIA often exhibited a further increase in activity, while RIB and AVA activity stayed at similar levels or decreased.
source: Within 30 s of NSM activation, AIA often exhibited a further increase in activity, while RIB and AVA activity stayed at similar levels or decreased.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C-G.

claim: As NSM activity rose and the animal entered the dwelling state, RIB and AVA activity declined sharply while AIA became correlated with NSM.
source: As NSM activity rose and the animal entered the dwelling state, RIB and AVA activity declined sharply while AIA became correlated with NSM.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5C-G.

claim: AIA activity co-varies with the forward-active neurons during roaming and with NSM at the onset of dwelling.
source: Thus, AIA activity co-varies with the forward-active neurons during roaming and with NSM at the onset of dwelling.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing that AIA activity is correlated with different neurons during different behavioral states.

claim: Roaming animals exhibited a rapid and transient decrease in speed upon AIA activation.
source: Roaming animals exhibited a rapid and transient decrease in speed upon AIA activation, while dwelling animals showed a gradual increase in speed upon AIA activation (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: Dwelling animals showed a gradual increase in speed upon AIA activation.
source: Roaming animals exhibited a rapid and transient decrease in speed upon AIA activation, while dwelling animals showed a gradual increase in speed upon AIA activation (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: Optogenetic activation of AIA can trigger the roaming-to-dwelling transition within a few seconds and promote entry into the roaming state upon tens of seconds of continued activation.
source: These results indicate that optogenetic activation of AIA can affect state transitions on two different time scales: triggering the roaming-to-dwelling transition within a few seconds and promoting entry into the roaming state upon tens of seconds of continued activation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing that AIA activation has different effects on roaming and dwelling animals.

claim: In tph-1 mutants, animals that were roaming pre-stimulation no longer displayed rapid entry into dwelling upon AIA activation and showed a higher probability of staying in the roaming state later into the stimulation.
source: For the tph-1 mutant, animals that were roaming pre-stimulation no longer displayed rapid entry into dwelling and showed a higher probability of staying in the roaming state later into the stimulation.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: tph-1 animals that were dwelling pre-stimulation displayed a higher probability of entering roaming compared to control animals upon AIA activation.
source: tph-1 animals that were dwelling pre-stimulation displayed a higher probability of entering roaming compared to control animals.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: tph-1 is critical for the effect of AIA activation on triggering entry into dwelling and for preventing AIA-induced entry into the roaming state.
source: These results suggest that tph-1 is critical for the effect of AIA activation on triggering entry into dwelling and for preventing AIA-induced entry into the roaming state.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing that AIA activation has different effects in tph-1 mutants compared to wild-type animals.

claim: AIA activation in pdfr-1 mutants that were dwelling pre-stimulation failed to promote transitions into roaming.
source: In contrast, AIA activation in pdfr-1 mutants that were dwelling pre-stimulation failed to promote transitions into roaming.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: AIA promotes dwelling via 5-HT signaling and promotes roaming via PDF signaling.
source: Together, these results suggest that AIA promotes dwelling via 5-HT signaling and promotes roaming via PDF signaling.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing that AIA activation has different effects in tph-1 and pdfr-1 mutants.

claim: AIA activation at lower light intensities primarily elicited roaming-to-dwelling transitions, while activation at higher intensities elicited dwelling-to-roaming transitions.
source: Indeed, AIA activation at lower light intensities primarily elicited roaming-to-dwelling transitions, while activation at higher intensities elicited dwelling-to-roaming transitions (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: AIA provides independent outputs to the PDF and 5-HT systems to control roaming and dwelling states, respectively.
source: Because the AIA-induced slowing response and speeding response depend on different neuromodulatory systems and can be elicited independently at different light intensities, these results are suggestive that AIA provides independent outputs to the PDF and 5-HT systems to control roaming and dwelling states, respectively (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing that AIA activation has different effects at different light intensities and in different mutants.

claim: AIA receives the majority of its synaptic inputs (~80%) from chemosensory neurons.
source: Based on the C. elegans connectome (Cook et al., 2019; White et al., 1986), AIA receives the majority of its synaptic inputs (~80%) from chemosensory neurons (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), many of which detect temporal changes in the concentrations of olfactory and gustatory cues (Chalasani et al., 2007; Larsch et al., 2015; Suzuki et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the C. elegans connectome (Cook et al., 2019; White et al., 1986) and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: AIA is activated by an increase in the concentration of attractive odorants present in bacterial food.
source: Previous work has shown that AIA is activated by an increase in the concentration of attractive odorants present in bacterial food (Larsch et al., 2015; Dobosiewicz et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Larsch et al., 2015; Dobosiewicz et al., 2019).

claim: In the absence of food, AIA promotes forward runs when animals detect increases in attractive odors.
source: In the absence of food, AIA promotes forward runs when animals detect increases in attractive odors (Larsch et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to a previous study (Larsch et al., 2015).

claim: In the patch foraging assay, wild-type animals exhibited directed motion toward the dense food patch and alternated between roaming and dwelling as they approached it.
source: In the patch foraging assay, wild-type animals exhibited directed motion toward the dense food patch and alternated between roaming and dwelling as they approached it (Figure 7A, bottom).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Compared to control plates without the dense food patch, animals in the patch foraging assay spent more time in the roaming state.
source: Compared to control plates without the dense food patch, animals in the patch foraging assay spent more time in the roaming state (Figure 7B), and biased their movement towards the dense food patch as they roamed (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Animals preferentially switched from roaming to dwelling when their direction of motion began to deviate away from the dense food patch.
source: Animals preferentially switched from roaming to dwelling when their direction of motion (measured as heading bias; Figure 7C) began to deviate away from the dense food patch (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7C-D.

claim: Dynamic changes in the concentration of food odors influences the transition rates between roaming and dwelling.
source: Because the animal's heading direction impacts the change in odor concentration that it experiences, these results indicate that dynamic changes in the concentration of food odors influences the transition rates between roaming and dwelling.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing that animals switch from roaming to dwelling when their heading direction deviates from the dense food patch.

claim: Chemosensation-defective tax-4 mutants subjected to the patch foraging assay failed to exhibit elevated roaming and failed to couple the roaming-to-dwelling transition with their direction of motion.
source: Consistent this interpretation, we found that chemosensation-defective tax-4 mutants (Komatsu et al., 1996) subjected to the patch foraging assay failed to exhibit elevated roaming and failed to couple the roaming-to-dwelling transition with their direction of motion (Figure 7B and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B and D and a citation to a previous study (Komatsu et al., 1996).

claim: AIA-silenced animals exhibited an overall decrease in roaming compared to wild-type animals in the patch foraging assay.
source: We found that AIA-silenced animals (AIA::unc-103gf) exhibited an overall decrease in roaming compared to wild-type animals and did not selectively enter dwelling states when their movement direction deviated away from the dense food patch (Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: AIA-silenced animals did not selectively enter dwelling states when their movement direction deviated away from the dense food patch.
source: We found that AIA-silenced animals (AIA::unc-103gf) exhibited an overall decrease in roaming compared to wild-type animals and did not selectively enter dwelling states when their movement direction deviated away from the dense food patch (Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: AIA is necessary for animals to display elevated roaming in the presence of a food odor gradient and for animals to couple their movement direction with roaming-to-dwelling transitions.
source: These results indicate that AIA is necessary for animals to display elevated roaming in the presence of a food odor gradient and for animals to couple their movement direction with roaming-to-dwelling transitions.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing that AIA-silenced animals have altered behavior in the patch foraging assay.

claim: pdfr-1 mutants failed to increase their roaming in the odor gradient but still displayed some coupling of the roaming-to-dwelling transition to their direction of motion.
source: We found that pdfr-1 mutants failed to increase their roaming in the odor gradient but still displayed some coupling of the roaming-to-dwelling transition to their direction of motion (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C-D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: tph-1 mutants displayed increased time in the roaming state but did not couple the roaming-to-dwelling transition to their direction of motion.
source: In contrast, tph-1 mutants displayed increased time in the roaming state but did not couple the roaming-to-dwelling transition to their direction of motion (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C-D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: In environments with uniformly-seeded bacterial food, AIA-silenced animals displayed a significant decrease in the fraction of time spent dwelling.
source: In both cases, AIA-silenced animals displayed a significant decrease in the fraction of time spent dwelling (Figure 7F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: AIA functions to promote the dwelling state in a constant sensory environment.
source: These results suggest that AIA functions to promote the dwelling state in a constant sensory environment.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing that AIA-silenced animals spend less time dwelling in uniform food environments.

claim: AIA can promote either roaming or dwelling, depending on the overall sensory environment.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that AIA can promote either roaming or dwelling, depending on the overall sensory environment.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing that AIA has different effects on roaming and dwelling in different sensory contexts.

claim: Mutual inhibition between the serotonergic NSM neuron and the 5-HT and PDF target neurons promotes the stability and mutual exclusivity of the neural activity patterns observed during roaming and dwelling.
source: By combining circuit imaging with genetic perturbations, we found that mutual inhibition between the serotonergic NSM neuron and the 5-HT and PDF target neurons promotes the stability and mutual exclusivity of the neural activity patterns observed during roaming and dwelling.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing that disrupting 5-HT or PDF signaling alters the persistence and mutual exclusivity of NSM and roaming-active neuron activity.

claim: The AIA sensory processing neuron that responds to food odors sends parallel outputs to both neuromodulatory systems and biases the network towards different states in different sensory contexts.
source: Furthermore, we found that the AIA sensory processing neuron that responds to food odors sends parallel outputs to both neuromodulatory systems and biases the network towards different states in different sensory contexts.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the data showing that AIA activation has different effects in different sensory contexts and in different mutants.

claim: This circuit architecture allows C. elegans to exhibit persistent roaming and dwelling states, while flexibly switching between them depending on the sensory context.
source: This circuit architecture allows C. elegans to exhibit persistent roaming and dwelling states, while flexibly switching between them depending on the sensory context.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the overall findings of the study.
